newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish parliament passes first anti-biker law.
newsitem.headline: Danish parliament passes first anti-biker law.

text.p: Denmark's parliament on Thursday approved the first of a planned series of laws designed to quash a bloody Nordic feud between the rival Hell's Angels and Bandidos motorcyle gangs.

The law, drafted amid growing grenade, gun and bomb attacks on biker clubhouses in the middle of residential districts, allows police to bar gang members from using properties that might draw fire from rivals, endangering innocent neighbours.
"This will create greater security for those living next to Hell's Angels and Bandidos strongholds," Justice Minister Bjoern Westh said after the vote.

A rush measure, announced by Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen last Tuesday and sent to parliament three days later, it received both its second and third readings on Thursday, winning support from both government and opposition benches.

Westh promised more new laws by November, giving police powers to search property and tap phones without a warrant and beefing up soft gun laws. Illegal firearm possession at present is likely to draw a prison term of two to four months.
There will also be measures to stop jailed bikers from terrorising other prison inmates and a review of police spending needs in light of the extra burden of the biker war.

On Friday Westh meets with colleagues from Finland, Norway and Sweden who will consider duplicating the Danish laws in their own countries and seek new joint initiatives to eradicate a plague which has struck them all.
Westh proposed the meeting after last Sunday's missile attack on the central Copenhagen headquarters of the Hell's Angels motorcycle gang, in which two people were killed.
Police regard the Bandidos, who have been battling the dominant Hell's Angels for close to three years, as the main suspect in Sunday's rocket attack.
Six of the 17 injured in the blast were still in hospital on Thursday, although all were out of danger, and police were hunting for three main suspects seen leaving the scene.

The shoulder-fired anti-tank rocket used in the attack and another abandoned unfired were stolen from army stores in neighbouring Sweden in 1994. Other missiles from the break-in were fired at two Hell's Angels' clubhouses in different areas of Denmark last April.
The association of Danish local authorities says there are now about 40 biker strongholds spread across the country.
Conflict between Hell's Angels and the Bandidos, both local offshoots of U.S. groups, arose almost as soon as the Bandidos set up shop in the region in the summer of 1993.

In February 1994 a member of the Hell's Angels-affiliated Rednecks died in a gunfight after walking -- reportedly by accident -- into a Bandidos meeting at a night club in the Swedish port of Helsingborg.

The then newly-elected president of the Bandidos, Mikael Ljunggren, was killed by a sniper as he rode his motorcycle north of the city in July 1995, in an ambush that investigators said could have been either a Hell's Angels attack or the work of fellow gang members opposed to his leadership.
In March this year, attackers shot dead a Bandidos leader in the Finnish capital, Helsinki, and a Danish Bandido died in an ambush outside Copenhagen airport 10 days later.
A Danish Bandidos member was fatally shot in the head near the Norwegian town of Drammen in July.
